title: Abram breaks the idols (Genesis Rabbah 38)
hookLine: a rabbinic story: young Abram smashes his father's idols and blames the biggest one
last: LECH LECHA — GO BEFORE YOU KNOW.

lines: A STICK IN THE BIG ONE'S HANDS.
LET YOUR EARS HEAR YOUR MOUTH.
cards: A shop full of statues, and a boy left in charge. Abram's father, Terah, makes idols and sells them, and one day he leaves young Abram to mind the shop. A customer comes in, and Abram asks how old he is.
Fifty, sixty. And you'd bow down to something made yesterday? The man leaves, embarrassed.

Then a woman brings a plate of fine flour as an offering for the gods. Abram picks up a stick, smashes every idol in the shop, and puts the stick in the hands of the biggest one. His father comes home.
What happened here? Abram says: a woman brought flour, the gods fought over who'd eat first, and the big one got up and smashed the rest. His father snaps: are you mocking me?

teach.h: NOT IN THE TORAH AT ALL.
teach.b: Here's the surprise: that story isn't in the Torah. It comes from Genesis Rabbah, a collection of rabbinic teachings on Genesis put together in the land of Israel.
It's a midrash, from the Hebrew root darash: to seek, to search, to dig into. It's how the rabbis read the Torah: asking questions of it and filling its silences.
God said to Abram, go. But why Abram? Genesis never says.
It tells us nothing about his childhood, or what he believed, or why God chose him. Midrash answers: because he questioned. He looked at a statue and asked whether it could really do anything.
The same book gives a second picture.
A man traveling sees a great house on fire. He wonders: can it be that this house has no owner? And the owner looks out and says, I am the owner.
So Abram looked at the world, beautiful and burning, asked who was responsible, and God answered. The Talmud says a verse never loses its plain meaning.
Midrash doesn't replace what the text says; it sits beside it, asking. So a reader can treasure a midrash and still know it's a midrash.
In that sense the tradition asks its own readers to question the statue, even a statue made of stories.

how: Jewish schools and families often tell the story of Abram and the idols when the Torah portion Lech Lecha is read, making clear that it comes from the midrash Genesis Rabbah rather than the Torah itself.

o: a story told word for word in Genesis
a rabbis' story that fills the Torah's gaps
a blessing said before eating bread

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the story of Abram smashing the idols is in the book of Genesis
it's a midrash, from Genesis Rabbah, a much later rabbinic collection. Genesis never tells of Abram's childhood.
Genesis explains why God chose Abram
it's silent. midrash fills the gap: he was a questioner.
the Talmud says a verse never loses its plain meaning
midrash sits beside the plain meaning; it doesn't replace it.

games.q: you're young Abram, alone in your father's idol shop. a woman has just left a plate of flour for the gods. what do you do?
o: leave the flour where it is.
smash the idols and put the stick in the biggest one's hands.
games.why: in the midrash, he smashes them and blames the biggest. when his father says idols can't do anything, Abram answers: let your ears hear what your mouth is saying.

practice: Pick one thing you just assume: that you're bad at math, that a neighbor doesn't like you, that you need your phone the moment you wake up, that things have to be done the way they've always been done.
Look at it the way Abram looked at the statue: can it really do what you think it does, and where did it come from? You don't have to smash anything; just ask.

wordCard.voice: Midrash. From darash, to seek. The rabbis' way of asking questions of the Torah and filling its silences with stories.

orig.note: Hebrew: a searching, from darash, to seek. rabbinic stories and teachings that read the Torah closely.

carryVoice: Your line: question the statue. In the midrash, Abram's first move is a question. On to tomorrow.
